problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y={x}^{3}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{3}}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})=3{x}^{2}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=9{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt[4]{3}}{x}^{3}\sqrt{1+9{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=1+9{x}^{4}\,⇒\,\text{d}u=36{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt[4]{3}}{x}^{3}\sqrt{1+9{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}(\frac{1}{36}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{18}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{18}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{27}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{27}.\end{aligned}
$$
